_note: THE INSTRUMENT BINDS TWO PEOPLE AND THE INTAKE CANNOT REPRESENT A THIRD.
D4.14 ran the 2->3 counterfactual on PARTNERSHIP_DEED. A user with three partners has two
routes and both fail, differently:
1. Supply partner_3_name. Sanitisation drops unknown keys and the third partner vanishes
from the document entirely, silently.
2. Describe the third partner in partner_roles free text. The name then appears in the
CAPITAL AND PROFIT clause and in NEITHER the identity clause NOR the signature block.
The second is the dangerous one. The deed recites a person as sharing capital and profits
while not making them a party to the instrument, and the capital clause still states a
two-way 60:40 split. Under the Indian Partnership Act 1932 that misstates the firm: s.4
defines partnership as the relation between persons who have agreed to share profits, and
s.25 makes every partner liable jointly and severally — a person who signs nothing is bound
by nothing the deed says, whatever the deed recites about their share.
WHY A NOTICE AND NOT A BLOCK. Extracting a partner count from free prose is unreliable, and
a false block on a correct two-partner deed would be worse than the defect. The rule fires
on an explicit ordinal — 'third partner', 'Partner 3', 'three partners' — which is a lexical
signal with a low false-positive rate and it is exactly the shape the counterfactual
produced. A user who wrote those words means them.
WHY THIS IS NOT THE REPAIR. It is a guard against shipping a wrong instrument while the real
repair is scoped. Representing N partners needs a repeating-entity type the intake model
does not have (zero collection-typed fields across all 40 families, no party index above 2
anywhere), AND N-party language in the 15 of 43 shared CORE clauses that say 'the other
Party'. Fields without language reproduce exactly the failure measured above: a name
recited, a person not bound.
Written entirely in the existing closed predicate vocabulary. No engine change.
AMENDED AFTER THE ROSTER LANDED. Route 1 above is now repaired: an indexed third principal
survives admission, reaches the identity clause and is signed for. Route 2 is not, and
cannot be — a name in prose is not a party, and inferring one from prose is the failure this
rule exists to report. So the assertion is no longer 'a third is unrepresentable' (a fact
about the system, which has changed) but 'the roster actually carries three' (a fact about
this document, which is what the reader needs). The notice now fires exactly when the deed
describes a principal it does not bind, and stays silent when the third partner is a party.

rules.description: The intake describes more principals than this instrument can make parties. The document names and is signed by two; anyone else mentioned in free text is recited without being bound.
rules.statutory_reference: Indian Partnership Act, 1932 - S.4; Indian Partnership Act, 1932 - S.25
rules.remedy: This instrument can name and bind two principals. A third must be added as a party in their own right — with their own name, address, identification and signature — which this intake cannot currently collect. Do not rely on a mention in free text: a person who signs nothing is bound by nothing, whatever the deed recites about their share.
